entries.note: Neither what constitutes collapse nor which revenue shifts count as its first signs is clear enough for a shared test.

entries.test: NVIDIA's customer concentration, GPU pricing and sales trends, and financial results would show whether its business depends on continually increasing purchases by four or five hyperscalers.
entries.note: The wallet metaphor refers plainly to spending with NVIDIA. The approximate customer count does not make the central dependency claim probabilistic.
“In real trouble” supplies no shared criterion for the predicted outcome. The separately stated commitment amount is checkable.

entries.test: Public fundraising records would establish the antecedent, and OpenAI's subsequent closure or liquidation would establish the predicted failure to survive.
entries.note: In context, this expresses an expectation of failure conditional on fundraising difficulty. No deadline is given.

entries.test: Public records of OpenAI's closure or liquidation would establish its failure to survive as an operating business.
entries.note: This is an emphatic expectation of failure in context. Continued operation for an arbitrary interval would not settle the undated forecast.

entries.test: Public financing terms, rental rates, capacity and operating costs would show whether full utilization still leaves both companies losing money because of the project's debt.
entries.note: This is a calculable claim about project economics at full capacity.

entries.test: Documented developer trials using the contemporary Claude Code, with timelines, working SaaS functionality and customer evaluations, would test the capability Zitron denies.
entries.note: The preceding quotation supplies the referent for his own explicit denial. The capability claim is testable independently of the accusation of lying.

entries.test: Share-price movements around AI announcements, alongside public investor commentary and market analyses, would test whether fears of LLM substitution drove incumbent software stocks down.
entries.note: Calling the belief a myth adds an assessment, but the asserted market effect has a plain empirical reading.

entries.test: Published accounts of impressive Claude Code projects, their working artifacts and comparisons with training-source projects would test the universal claim, with a substantive original project providing a counterexample.
entries.note: “You've read” plainly addresses circulating public examples. Unavailable training details make verification harder, not inherently impossible.

entries.test: Reproducible trials of the contemporary Claude Code using a simple CRM request, followed by deployment, functionality, security and compliance checks, would test what it delivers without engineering intervention.
entries.note: “I assume” qualifies the presumed training sources, whereas the normalization moves that hedge onto the claim of no differentiation. The passage otherwise describes current capabilities through a generic example.
The causal premise that LLMs “don't know anything” has no shared empirical definition of knowledge. Particular false compliance assurances would not settle that premise.
The source judges whether the sell-off has a rational basis; the normalization instead asserts its only actual cause. Those are different commitments.

entries.test: A representative set of enthusiastic Claude Code articles, their authors' public affiliations and software-building records, and the demonstrated projects would test this characterization.
entries.note: The insults accompany factual claims about most authors and their examples. Those claims remain open to public counterevidence.
